This strikes me as a little too serious. While I can certainly see Duke painting portraits of himself with the tears of orphans, overdramatic idiot that he is, I can’t read about it without laughing at the sheer dramatic ridiculousness of such a thing. I figured he was just gonna eat the kids, since they were presumably virgins.

I also think you have too many “y”s in people’s names, and that using a real city instead of “Noxus” would be better. The Foundationverse mostly resembles the real world on the surface, not some fantasy setting.

+ show block
– hide block

The thing about the names leads into the biggest criticism: there is nothing SCP about this story. I could’ve conceivably read the same thing about any fictional vampire, and the usage of a fictional city and unrealistic names deepens the impression that this story is supposed to be something else but you decided to slap Duke on it and post it here instead. That might be okay if the character was still recognizably Duke, but he’s got weird powers we’ve never heard of before (turning fountains into portals) and acts different from the asshole in the file and the tale.

I commend your bravery in trying to write a tale about an SCP-D, but remember this thing was decommissioned for a reason: it sucked (pun intended). If you want to write something serious about Duke, it’s got to be very much not sucky, and that’s hard.

Hello hello socialdeath! Welcome to the Wiki! I'm Ralliston, a site author and a member of the Community Outreach Team - with this helpful little comment, I'll try to help you find your way around the site and link a bunch of useful places and links that will help you in your SCP journey.

It's awesome to see you want to contribute to the site - I really can't wait to see what you'll come up with. If you'll want to look for helpful resources filled to the brim with content that is created to guide you through your writing journey, you'll want to click that little red collapsible at the bottom of this comment - there, you'll find a plethora of useful resources created for the purpose of guiding new members of the site towards guides and other resources which will definitely help you improve your writing and seek help on it.

Without further ado though, let's click the collapsible, shall we? :)

+ show block
– hide block

If you're going to try your hand at writing, try out our Sandbox. You can make yourself a page here to store your drafts, which are in-works articles. Using it, you can link the drafts to reviewers to get their opinions on them before posting. It really helps everyone out a lot.

For brainstorming concepts, try out the Ideas and Brainstorming forum. You can run your ideas by experienced members of the community if you need help refining and fleshing out your concept. It's a very helpful little place for when you want to start your writing journey, especially when you're not sure if the idea is all that great.

If you have a draft ready, make a thread in the Drafts and Critiques forum. Remember to check the stickied posts in the relevant thread for guidelines on how best to use each forum. You can also try the IRC chat for real-time feedback.

From site usage to writing tips, the Guide Hub contains a wealth of resources geared towards helping members produce successful articles. Within the Guides, you will find useful information written by experienced members of the site for the use of newer ones.

The more time you take to familiarize yourself with the SCP style, the drafting process, and the community, the greater your chances are for success! Remember - there is no rush to writing - take your time! The more time you spend on fleshing your ideas out, the more your chance of success becomes!

As far as reading is concerned, you might want to check out Top Rated New Pages, which will display the most popular recent articles. It's helpful to keep up with what's being received well by the community to implement into your very own writing. Alternatively, you might want to look at the User Curated Lists page, where members of the community list and rank their favorite articles in different genres and themes, showing which attempts at such are successful and what the community likes.

Best of luck with your future contributions to the site! I hope you enjoy your time here as much as we do! If you have any more questions, feel free to message me here on Wikidot or on the IRC chats!

item.title: This Author Post is Sponsored by the Koalalition
item.content:encoded:
Hello! Veralta's here with a new SCP about koalas, nature, the future of Australia, and intricate worldbuilding based on the beliefs of aboriginal Australian people like the Bundjalung and the Eora. Consider this SCP a free New Year trip through Australia, and a little bit of a crash course on the Australian condition.

Also, it's linked to Ralliston's Obearwatch Command; fun fact, all of these started when he threw the word "Koalalition" at me, and I said, "Hmm… uwah, this looks interesting". I initially planned out a short article with a gimmick and a punchline.

But then, I realized I had to dive deep into the waterhole.

The aboriginal Australian belief system, also called Dreamtime1, is very complex and interesting. It would be a shame if I just went with a silly punchline when aboriginal culture, with its mix of hopes and dreams for Australia, needs a chance to shine here.

Lastly, consider this article as a piece dedicated to Australians and wildlife - such as the koalas themselves - who have been affected by the severe bushfires. As a Filipino youth, I couldn't do much to be honest, aside from raising awareness. I tried to stay true to the myths' essence while adding my style of writing to them, while I researched news about the bushfires.

All in all, though, please enjoy this SCP, and I wish a Happy New Year - and more happy years - to come for all of us!

Special thanks to Ralliston2, Meisteroni, DrChandra, Rose the Changeling , for concept checking and making my narrative is solid. Dysadron and caspian2 also have my gratitude for their comprehensively good LBL and critique. Last but not the least, I also want to give a deserved shoutout to Dr Balthazaar for providing guidance on Australian beliefs and culture. You guys are amazing!

Footnotes
1. By the way, this word does not cover what the beliefs really mean, and while dreaming is a part of the culture, it is not just that. Additionally, the word "Dreamtime" may even be just a mistranslation of words meant for deities.
2. Bear goes rawr :p

item.title: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) Joke SCP - mind-influencing game code
item.content:encoded:
I'm not really a fan of an idea that boils actual addictions down to 'oh it's an anomaly', particularly ones that can be as quietly harmful to people as video game addictions can be.

Beyond this, the narrative feels…unfocussed? It kinda flits around various ideas: the behavioural patterns of the SCP, the way it affects players, the list of games it was part of; and it feels like these ideas never really come together to form a single, cohesive whole. It also feels like this could really do with a like…single affected player as the focus character, like, someone we can see slipping into worse and worse patterns of behaviour and whose plight is empathetic in a way that fills us with dread as we see them descend towards some final outcome that's terrible; but my concern is that the effect of the SCP is too compulsive for this to work well. That is to say: the SCP is effectively forcing them to become addicted, so there's no real like, choice or ability for them to like resist this or anything; whereas if the SCP was more…'seductive', then you can really like, have them be conflicted about whether they should stop and really give the narrative the conflict it needs that way.

I don't think it necessarily needs to be focussed in this specific manner; but it does feel like it all needs to come together in a way that makes it feel like this is telling a single, coherent story and it doesn't quite yet do that, for me.

item.title: Re: SCP Concept: Guitar Hero
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

Not really a fan of this as a whole. It feels…too much like a generic murder monster withy a lot of additional complexity that just, isn't very interesting to me; which isn't helped by the central narrative section just expanding more on what the SCP does. What I really want to see out of a pitch like this is an indication you've considered how you can explore what the SCP does in an interesting way, or like have built up some kind of story about the SCP and the Foundation's interactions with it that really emphasises why it's interesting to read about.

As an aside, murder monsters aren't inherently a bad idea to write about as a SCP; but they do present challenges to writing. Namely, you aren't trying to write a DnD Monster Manual style entry, and danger alone isn't interesting; so you have to figure out how you can make the danger feel interesting. Often, this is easiest by putting characters the reader cares about in danger (even in a very stripped down way e.g. SCP-3794, or providing clear stakes to the danger and having the threat be like, present. It's also possible to make it work if the danger is sufficiently interesting alone: something like SCP-5852 is a great example of that; where the core is very simple but the threat is effective nevertheless.

I think SCP-XXXX-ɑ is the best example of my issue with this: rather than relying on the user of the guitar being like 'wow I'm great at this I have to keep playing this', you've added a chemical it emits that basically forces people to keep playing it; and it feels like added complexity that doesn't actually make this more interesting. In general: it's a lot more interesting when people choose to do things instead of being forced to by a SCP because the agency that choosing grants allows you to really explore why someone would choose to do it and the conflict that choosing to continue doing something even once you begin to see the dangerous effects come in creates.

This isn't to say that's the only issue: the issue with this pitch at it's core is that instead of keeping the anomaly simple and doing something interesting with it, you've extended it's behaviour and the range of anomalous things it can do in an attempt at making it more interesting. My general advice for anomaly design is 'you should be able to describe what the anomaly does fully in one sentence': it doesn't apply always, but severely limiting the scope of the concept like that allows you to really focus on why the anomaly is interesting and how it's effects affect the world at large in an easier way.

item.title: Re: Seeking Greenlight : The Man with the Bowler Hat
item.content:encoded:
1) It sounds like you're trying to set him up to be the opposite of SCP-343.

2) Most of what you have as "Hook" is just more description. This character lacks a reason for people to be interested in him and for him to be a part of the SCP-U; the question is how does he fit into the greater universe, and what does he do that's different from any other SCP. You have a part of it (answering a question about anything, including SCPs), but you need to build on that a bit.

3) Speaking of: If he has access to all of this knowledge, why does he ask the one question? Sure he can create some chaos with the right question, but what does he get out of besides relieving boredom> Or is that it? You need to point out what he gets.

4) Also, what are these "mind fights"? How these happen, and what happens, needs to be better defined.

item.title: Dark Dogs Ritual
item.content:encoded:
Greenlight: yes

Page layout: SCP article

Elevator pitch: Stray dogs goes into a forest to commence a ritual involving a black dog with the unidentifiable breed to have it fed. It only comes once three weeks; when that happens, the Dark dog will choose which dog to eat based on its bravery (fending off the creature). It will attack humans, will kill them but will not eat them.

+ Central Narrative
- Central Narrative

Central Narrative: Dr Fox observes them afore and tries to understand why these dogs are circling one particular spot, first time watching the dogs the research team had no idea about the three-week circle. So when the last day of the third week hits a giant dog appears and begins to chase the dogs around trying to find one that is stronger, all of the dogs dispersed its attacked spot where the researcher was and started to hunt them down. Dr Fox attempted to fend off the creature but was dragged under a car by three other dogs. Same with another researcher (they all hide) They hid under the car for 7 hours while the creature continues to hunt after dogs until it found one that began to bark at it, it ate the dog and disappeared back to the forest.

Later, Dr Fox wants to learn why one specific spot, so they dig the area and found skeletons of a man (named Damian) and a dog. Knowing this, they investigate the whole forest and learns that the bodies were murder victims. After extensive investigation, the lead points to his roommate. It said that Damian left his dorm to walk in the morning with his dog on 01/01/2014 and never returned. The roommate ends up being the one that killed Damian and the dog. While in containment, the stray dogs started to circle the site and caused containment breach, and the dark dog bites off Dr Fox’s hand (severely injuring her). And she learns that the dog and Damian’s skeletons when together were the ones that were manifesting the dark dog.

Hook/Attention: a little jab on the idea that dogs can sense evil spirits.

item.title: Re: The Monastery of the Weaponsmith (seeking greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

My, concern with this is that it feels a little too focussed on 'the monks have cool weapons!' as the core interesting thing here: while having the monks have cool weapons isn't a terrible idea, it seems… unlikely that it will be interesting enough to carry a full article. Like, at the end of the day, you're really trying to write an interesting short story about the SCP, not a DnD style magic weapon (or, in this case, magic weapons).

A lot of this feels like it's building up to the Foundation busting into the Monastery finally after a lot of attempts, and like…my twofold concern is that I don't know if you're actually going to have them succeed; and if they do succeed, I'm not sure there's enough pay off for the build up? The first is an issue because like, if there's no closure to the narrative, it'll feel really unsatisfying when someone reaches the end: the whole thing is built around the conflict between the monks and the foundation, but without that conflict being resolved, it'll just feel…unfinished. I'm also concerned that there's a lack of stakes to this: the Foundation doesn't really have a lot of motivation to break into this monastery beyond the standard 'the foundation loves to break into places' motive. The second is an issue because like, you have to make all the effort the Foundation puts in to get into this place feel worthwhile: the harder it is, the bigger it has to feel when they succeed.

This…kinda feels like it's really just an excuse to have a lot of cool action scenes without a lot of reason for a reader to get invested in the scenes?

item.title: Music makes you lose control - Declass attempt
item.content:encoded:
The article is well written, but I find the narrative hard to understand. I think an official declassification would be very good.

+ Attempt at D-class-if-cation
- Probably wrong in some places

The red portions of the article indicate a change from the original article. Let's look at the original text first.

Originally, two personnel talk about the technology and how SCP-3955 is recorded. By putting a music creating AI in a WARP Train from Library of Ruina box that accelerates time, SCP-3955 will be observed in the created music. A few examples are provided, and the article ends.

Except for the mysterious edits that have been placed in the article. SCP-3955 doesn't need to be contained or concealment, but its now an Apollyon class SCP. Whoever is editing this article doesn't want the anomaly to be referred as an SCP. Re-reading the article, it seems like ██████ ████ (one of the scientists behind the anomaly) is trying to stop a rogue AI (the AI being tested to make music) from changing the document.

██████ ████ has a portion of their text in the Conprocs, as there's a note that unauthorized changes are to be reverted immediately. To me, this edit in the Conprocs is very different from the other edits. Potentially, they might be losing control of the entire article in addendum 03. This addendum was made when the article was last updated, and the editor's words begin to become heavily blackboxed. Quote:

"On April 12th, at 4:02 pm, Dr. ████ followed up on a hunch regarding ███-3955's possible connections to a series of abstract, deep-space transmissions found in CRYSTAL-INE's database. Findings indicate ████ ██ ███ ██ █████ █████ ██████ ██ ████ ███ ███ ████ █████████ ██████ ███ █████ ██ █ ████ ██ █████.

There are to be no further additions to this document."

Once the AI takes control of the article, it starts heavily blackboxing everything related to the SCP Foundation. The reason for this is that the AI has gained some sentience. This is evident in addendum 04, where the AI begins to feel emotion and develops advanced thoughts. At first, it has its basic functions listed and it begins to become wary of its purpose. It starts going insane and starts questioning music, even giving names to its "cyclical" music processes. Once the AI finds the document, it tries to change it dramatically, even putting a warning in the Conprocs to stop testing. Due to its lack of access privileges, the article remains in its editing phase.

…Re-reading this, the rogue AI thin is probably all incorrect. It's just strange that edits are being made after 16:02, as addendum 04 has a log from 16:04. If this really is an Apollyon, is it talking about how music is unstoppable? Or did the AI find out that SCP-3955 is very dangerous for humans?

Probably wasted time writing that, but eh. +1

item.title: Re: Seeking Greenlight - Self-Casting Spell
item.content:encoded:
This is definitely a weird concept. The problem here is that you're going to have to define a magic system, at least the extreme basics of it, and then how these spells gained sentience and took on human form. Making it harder is that you've apparently decided to base it on the Catholic system, which is mostly defensive (thaumaturgy is more of a defensive art than anything else), rather than a more dynamic pagan system (which would actually be more likely for the sybiraks given when they were exiled to Syberia).

It doesn't help that spells in the SCP-U are based more on defense, such as protection and keeping SCP down.

Basically, you have what amounts to a new race that you're trying to describe, and so you need to have a pretty good hook. Figure out why people should care for it, why it matters, and go from there.

item.title: Re: LOOKING FOR GREENLIGHT/SCP Early concept: the greatest artist
item.content:encoded:
A little verbose on the history front, but I think we're getting somewhere.

+ show block
– hide block

humans always found a need to do art, of course there were different kinds of art but it was always art, so it tried to copy us thourhgt the years and believed that replicating our art is the way to comprehend what is "being human" so it currently is in this endless loop it tries to make art

This is probably as close to motivation as we can get; a desire to be human by means of expressing what it believes to be human expressions. The additional "loss of identity" aspect is a bit so-so, but it's workable. This is good!

I think the narrative of the article could revolve around the scientist breaking it's current delusional state of existence where he is so deep in the whole "Mimicing humans" thing it thinks each one of its forms are actual people with actual life historys, and after that facade is broken they could get him psychological assistance.

I really like this idea! It doesn't necessarily need to be something that the doctor means to do. Maybe they just get fed up with the mistaken identity act and they verbally lash out. You could play with that a little, too; the entity could use the doctor's outrage as it's own inspiration and couple it with realization of what it truly is.

i plan to write this all way more subtly than here ofc but that's what I have so far

Subtlety is important, yes, but you should also make sure that you don't sacrifice your core story elements by underplaying them. This is fiction. It is equally important to play up moments to engage the reader.

I'm glad to see that you've taken the time to rethink your approach to this idea. I'm not sure how much more I can do on the brainstorming side here, so it might be better to see how you've decided to execute it. Consider this a greenlight. You do need to two to use the Drafts Forums, so if that is something you'd like to pursue, I suggest reaching out to another reviewer, perhaps by utilizing our Butterfly Squad Roster.

Good luck.

item.title: Re: Looking for greenlight
item.content:encoded:
Hi author!

Here's the crit
here it be

Let me start off by saying that I do see the humor in how weird the basics of this concept are. The imagery of infectious hummingbirds is compelling.

However, I don't see this concept working as is. SCP articles are typically stories disguised as descriptive files. What you have here is a fairly straightforward "Monster Manual" entry, in which you present an idea for a creature and leave it at that. While that may have been a popular approach in the earlier days of the site, I think you'll find that things have progressed somewhat.

It's important to think about the story that your anomaly can tell, moreso even than the details of your anomaly's effects. I would recommend starting with a narrative you find interesting and then building an anomaly around it instead of vice versa. While you're at it, I'd also recommend checking out some Series VI skips just to get an idea of how story-driven most modern articles are.

Have a good day!

item.title: Re: Head of Life
item.content:encoded:
The problem is that this is a classic "thing that does a thing" but that's about it. It's sort of cool in that it evolves as he ages, but then you do nothing with it.

Something to consider is that his life could be linked to the creatures on his head; you could predict how old he would be when he dies by comparing which age the creatures are in and extrapolating (or about early 30s).

Also, a number of scientists would be interesting in studying the creatures in order to get an idea of how evolution works; they could perform experiments to see how they would affect the creatures' evolution.

The bottom line is that there no real hook; there's no real reason to care about this as you described. That needs to be worked on. Otherwise, it's just an interesting idea.
